    .format("delta")
    .partitionBy("event_date")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/chk/clickstream")
    .option("delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite", "true")
    .toTable("clickstream"))

# (b) + (c) Scheduled maintenance job (run daily via a Workflow)
# Compact the last 2 days of partitions and cluster by user_id
spark.sql("""
  OPTIMIZE clickstream
  WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 2 DAYS
  ZORDER BY (user_id)
""")

# Reclaim storage: remove unreferenced files older than the retention window
spark.sql("VACUUM clickstream RETAIN 168 HOURS")

lineByLine: to_date('event_ts') derives the partition column event_date. writeStream ... partitionBy('event_date') physically lays data out in per-day directories, enabling partition pruning for date-filtered queries and per-day maintenance. optimizeWrite reduces the number of files each micro-batch produces. checkpointLocation gives exactly-once restartable streaming. The maintenance OPTIMIZE is scoped with WHERE event_date >= current_date() - 2 days so it only bin-packs recently written (still-fragmented) partitions instead of rewriting history, and ZORDER BY (user_id) clusters that data for fast user-filtered reads. VACUUM RETAIN 168 HOURS (7 days) deletes data files no longer referenced by the current table version and older than the retention window, reclaiming storage from compacted-away small files while keeping a 7-day time-travel/safety window.
timeComplexity: Streaming write cost scales with per-batch volume. OPTIMIZE rewrites only the matched recent partitions, O(bytes in those partitions); the WHERE scope keeps it bounded. VACUUM is O(files) of listing and deleting unreferenced files.
spaceComplexity: Compaction transiently doubles space for rewritten partitions until VACUUM runs. Steady-state storage is bounded because VACUUM continually reclaims old versions; without it the table would grow unbounded.

alternativeApproaches.title: Auto compaction instead of scheduled OPTIMIZE
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Enable delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact so Delta compacts small files automatically right after writes, reducing or eliminating the need for a scheduled OPTIMIZE. You still schedule VACUUM for storage reclamation.

alternativeApproaches.title: Liquid Clustering (no explicit partitions)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: On newer Delta, use CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id) instead of static partitioning. Liquid Clustering adapts file layout to data and query patterns, avoids tiny partition folders, and removes the need to choose partition granularity up front while still giving good pruning.

followUps.question: Why partition by event_date rather than by event_hour or user_id?
followUps.answer: Partitioning granularity must match query patterns and produce reasonably sized partitions (ideally at least ~1 GB each). event_date matches typical time-range queries and keeps the partition count manageable. event_hour would create 24x more, smaller partitions, worsening the small-file problem and metadata overhead. user_id is high cardinality (potentially millions of values), which would explode the number of tiny partitions and devastate performance. For fine-grained filtering on user_id, use ZORDER or Liquid Clustering within the date partitions rather than partitioning on it.

followUps.question: What happens if you never run VACUUM, and how do you pick the retention period?
followUps.answer: Without VACUUM, every OPTIMIZE, UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE leaves the old, now-unreferenced files on storage forever, so storage grows unbounded and listing slows even though the logical table is small. Pick the retention to cover your longest needs: the maximum time travel window you want plus a buffer for any long-running concurrent readers/streams that might still reference old files. The default 7 days is a safe common choice; shorten it only when storage cost matters and you have confirmed no consumers need older versions, since vacuuming files still in use can break those operations.
